claim: SNARE complex disassembly by the ATPase NSF is essential for neurotransmitter release and other membrane trafficking processes.
source: SNARE complex disassembly by the ATPase NSF is essential for neurotransmitter release and other membrane trafficking processes.
evidence: This is a statement about the essential role of NSF in biological processes, drawing from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: For ternary neuronal SNARE complexes, disassembly proceeds in a single step within 100 msec.
source: For ternary neuronal SNARE complexes, disassembly proceeds in a single step within 100 msec.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations from the single-molecule FRET assay described in the manuscript.

claim: Short-lived disassembled states (<0.32 s) correspond to failed disassembly or immediate reassembly.
source: The long-lived states represent fully disassembled SNARE complex, while the short-lived states correspond to failed disassembly or immediate reassembly.
evidence: This interpretation is based on analysis of the dwell time distributions from the smFRET experiments.

claim: Long-lived disassembled states (≥0.32 s) represent fully disassembled SNARE complex.
source: The long-lived states represent fully disassembled SNARE complex, while the short-lived states correspond to failed disassembly or immediate reassembly.
evidence: This interpretation is based on analysis of the dwell time distributions from the smFRET experiments.

claim: High ionic strength reduces the disassembly rate of SNARE complexes.
source: Either high ionic strength or decreased αSNAP concentration reduces the disassembly rate while increasing the frequency of short-lived states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the effect of varying NaCl concentrations on disassembly kinetics.

claim: Decreased αSNAP concentration reduces the disassembly rate of SNARE complexes.
source: Either high ionic strength or decreased αSNAP concentration reduces the disassembly rate while increasing the frequency of short-lived states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the effect of varying αSNAP concentrations on disassembly kinetics.

claim: High ionic strength increases the frequency of short-lived disassembled states.
source: Either high ionic strength or decreased αSNAP concentration reduces the disassembly rate while increasing the frequency of short-lived states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the effect of varying NaCl concentrations on the population of short-lived states.

claim: Decreased αSNAP concentration increases the frequency of short-lived disassembled states.
source: Either high ionic strength or decreased αSNAP concentration reduces the disassembly rate while increasing the frequency of short-lived states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the effect of varying αSNAP concentrations on the population of short-lived states.

claim: NSF is capable of disassembling anti-parallel ternary SNARE complexes.
source: NSF is also capable of disassembling anti-parallel ternary SNARE complexes, implicating it in quality control.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using anti-parallel reporting FRET label pairs showing NSF-mediated disassembly of improperly assembled SNARE complexes.

claim: NSF's ability to disassemble anti-parallel SNARE complexes implicates it in quality control.
source: NSF is also capable of disassembling anti-parallel ternary SNARE complexes, implicating it in quality control.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that NSF can disassemble improperly assembled SNARE complexes.

claim: Complexin-1 competes with αSNAP binding to the SNARE complex.
source: Finally, complexin-1 competes with αSNAP binding to the SNARE complex; addition of complexin-1 has an effect similar to that of decreasing the αSNAP concentration, possibly differentially regulating cis and trans SNARE complexes disassembly.
evidence: This is supported by competition binding experiments showing that Cpx reduces αSNAP binding to SNARE complexes.

claim: Addition of complexin-1 has an effect similar to that of decreasing the αSNAP concentration on SNARE complex disassembly.
source: Finally, complexin-1 competes with αSNAP binding to the SNARE complex; addition of complexin-1 has an effect similar to that of decreasing the αSNAP concentration, possibly differentially regulating cis and trans SNARE complexes disassembly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing similar effects of Cpx addition and reduced αSNAP concentration on disassembly kinetics.

claim: Complexin-1 possibly differentially regulates cis and trans SNARE complexes disassembly.
source: Finally, complexin-1 competes with αSNAP binding to the SNARE complex; addition of complexin-1 has an effect similar to that of decreasing the αSNAP concentration, possibly differentially regulating cis and trans SNARE complexes disassembly.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observed effects of Cpx on NSF-mediated disassembly.

claim: SNAREs from opposing membranes assemble into a trans SNARE complex and provide the energy for membrane fusion upon zippering into a cis SNARE complex.
source: SNAREs from opposing membranes assemble into a trans SNARE complex and provide the energy for membrane fusion upon zippering into a cis SNARE complex (Sutton et al., 1998; Weber et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research establishing this mechanism.

claim: The cis SNARE complex is disassembled by the ATPase N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor (NSF) in combination with SNAP adapter proteins.
source: Subsequently, the cis SNARE complex is disassembled by the ATPase N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor (NSF) (Block et al., 1988; Malhotra et al., 1988) in combination with SNAP (soluble NSF attachment protein) adapter proteins (Weidman et al., 1989).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research establishing this mechanism.

claim: There are three SNAP isoforms: αSNAP, βSNAP, and γSNAP.
source: While there are three SNAP isoforms—αSNAP, βSNAP, and γSNAP (Clary et al., 1990; Nishiki et al., 2001; Söllner et al., 1993a; Whiteheart et al., 1992; Wilhelm et al., 2014)—most in vitro studies have been carried out with αSNAP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research identifying these isoforms.

claim: Most in vitro studies of SNARE complex disassembly have been carried out with αSNAP.
source: While there are three SNAP isoforms—αSNAP, βSNAP, and γSNAP (Clary et al., 1990; Nishiki et al., 2001; Söllner et al., 1993a; Whiteheart et al., 1992; Wilhelm et al., 2014)—most in vitro studies have been carried out with αSNAP.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature and experimental practices in the field.

claim: Prior to ATP hydrolysis and together with SNAPs and the SNARE complex, NSF forms the so-called 20S complex.
source: Prior to ATP hydrolysis and together with SNAPs and the SNARE complex, NSF forms the so-called 20S complex; the structural details of the starting point for this process have been described previously (Zhao et al., 2015; White et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: NSF and the SNAPs disassemble the binary complex consisting of the t-SNAREs syntaxin-1A and SNAP-25A.
source: NSF and the SNAPs also disassemble other configurations of the SNARE complex, such as the binary complex consisting of the t-SNAREs syntaxin-1A and SNAP-25A (Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Combined with Munc13 and Munc18, NSF, SNAPs, syntaxin-1A, and SNAP-25A comprise an essential system that produces and maintains a pool of fusogenic trans SNARE complexes.
source: Combined with the essential synaptic proteins Munc13 and Munc18, these four proteins comprise an essential system that produces and maintains a pool of fusogenic trans SNARE complexes (Lai et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Complexin has the highest affinity for the full-length ternary SNARE complex among SNARE-interacting proteins.
source: Among these proteins, Cpx has by far the highest affinity for the full-length ternary SNARE complex (KD ≈ 10–100 nM, (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2007; Pabst et al., 2002), higher than that of αSNAP for the SNARE complex (KD ≈ 1.5 μM, (Vivona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous binding affinity measurements.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) of complexin for the full-length ternary SNARE complex is approximately 10-100 nM.
source: Among these proteins, Cpx has by far the highest affinity for the full-length ternary SNARE complex (KD ≈ 10–100 nM, (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2007; Pabst et al., 2002), higher than that of αSNAP for the SNARE complex (KD ≈ 1.5 μM, (Vivona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous binding affinity measurements.

claim: The dissociation constant (KD) of αSNAP for the SNARE complex is approximately 1.5 μM.
source: Among these proteins, Cpx has by far the highest affinity for the full-length ternary SNARE complex (KD ≈ 10–100 nM, (Choi et al., 2016; Li et al., 2007; Pabst et al., 2002), higher than that of αSNAP for the SNARE complex (KD ≈ 1.5 μM, (Vivona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous binding affinity measurements.

claim: Complexin plays a critical role in neurotransmitter release by activating synchronous release upon the arrival of action potential in the synaptic terminal.
source: Functionally, Cpx plays a critical role in neurotransmitter release by activating synchronous release upon the arrival of action potential in the synaptic terminal and by regulating spontaneous release (Mohrmann et al., 2015; Trimbuch and Rosenmund, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Complexin regulates spontaneous neurotransmitter release.
source: Functionally, Cpx plays a critical role in neurotransmitter release by activating synchronous release upon the arrival of action potential in the synaptic terminal and by regulating spontaneous release (Mohrmann et al., 2015; Trimbuch and Rosenmund, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claim: Complexin forms a bipartite complex with the ternary SNARE complex.
source: Structurally, Cpx forms a bipartite complex with the ternary SNARE complex (Chen et al., 2002), and, together with the Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin, it forms a tripartite complex that represents a primed prefusion state of these synaptic proteins (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural studies.

claim: Complexin, together with synaptotagmin, forms a tripartite complex with the SNARE complex that represents a primed prefusion state.
source: Structurally, Cpx forms a bipartite complex with the ternary SNARE complex (Chen et al., 2002), and, together with the Ca2+ sensor synaptotagmin, it forms a tripartite complex that represents a primed prefusion state of these synaptic proteins (Zhou et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous structural studies.

claim: A previous single-molecule study monitored at most one disassembly event per individual SNARE complex.
source: A previous single-molecule study monitored at most one disassembly event per individual SNARE complex (Ryu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The linked SNARE complex enables monitoring of multiple rounds of SNARE complex disassembly and reassembly.
source: We developed an new single-molecule approach using a linked SNARE complex where the three SNARE proteins are fused by long, flexible linkers (Gao et al., 2012; Zorman et al., 2014) to enable monitoring of multiple rounds of SNARE complex disassembly and reassembly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing multiple transitions in smFRET traces and citations to previous work on linked SNARE complexes.

claim: The structure of the L-20S complex is similar to a recent high-resolution structure of the 20S complex prepared with full-length soluble SNAP-25A and full-length soluble syntaxin-1A but without synthetic linkers between the SNARE proteins.
source: The structure of the L-20S complex is similar to a recent high-resolution structure of the 20S complex prepared with full-length soluble SNAP-25A and full-length soluble syntaxin-1A but without synthetic linkers between the SNARE proteins (White et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the cryo-EM structure determined in this study with a previously published structure.

claim: Both the L-20S complex and the 20S complex with full-length SNAP-25A show two bound αSNAP molecules.
source: Both structures show two bound αSNAP molecules rather than four as seen in the structure of the 20S complex lacking the native linker between the two SNAP-25A SNARE motifs (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cryo-EM structure and comparison with previous structures.

claim: The 20S complex lacking the native linker between the two SNAP-25A SNARE motifs shows four bound αSNAP molecules.
source: Both structures show two bound αSNAP molecules rather than four as seen in the structure of the 20S complex lacking the native linker between the two SNAP-25A SNARE motifs (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study.

claim: The reduction of the number of αSNAP molecules bound to the 20S complex was confirmed by a gel-based assay.
source: This reduction of the number of αSNAP molecules bound to the 20S complex was also confirmed by a gel-based assay, where the 20S complex was formed in the presence and absence of the native linker of SNAP-25A (amino acid range 86–119) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from SDS-PAGE analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The αSNAP:NSF protein ratio decreased by a factor of two when the native linker of SNAP-25A was included.
source: Consistent with the cryo-EM structures, the αSNAP:NSF protein ratio decreased by a factor of two when the native linker of SNAP-25A was included (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantification of protein bands from SDS-PAGE gels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The two αSNAP molecules primarily bind to a portion of the surface of the SNARE complex formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2.
source: In the resulting model, the two αSNAP molecules primarily bind to a portion of the surface of the SNARE complex formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 (Figure 1B), leaving the surface formed by SNAP-25A largely accessible.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure of the L-20S complex shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The surface of the SNARE complex formed by SNAP-25A is largely accessible in the L-20S complex.
source: In the resulting model, the two αSNAP molecules primarily bind to a portion of the surface of the SNARE complex formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 (Figure 1B), leaving the surface formed by SNAP-25A largely accessible.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure of the L-20S complex shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The similarities between the L-20S complex and the 20S complex suggest minimal structural perturbation due to the presence of the synthetic linkers.
source: Taken together, these similarities suggest minimal structural perturbation due to the presence of the synthetic linkers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural comparison between the L-20S complex and the 20S complex.

claim: The disassembly rate for L-SNARE-CC molecules is 1/(14.3 ± 3.7) s−1.
source: In order to calculate the disassembly rate for the L-SNARE-CC molecules that transition from the long-lived high FRET efficiency state, we fit a first-order exponential function to the high FRET efficiency dwell time histogram (Figure 2G, left panel) for times longer than 0.56 s, resulting in a rate of 1/(14.3 ± 3.7) s−1.
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data by fitting the dwell time histogram.

claim: The disassembly rate of L-SNARE-CC is comparable to that previously observed by smFRET experiments using unlinked SNARE complexes reconstituted in liposomes (1/14 s−1).
source: This disassembly rate is comparable to that previously observed by smFRET experiments using unlinked SNARE complexes reconstituted in liposomes (1/14 s−1) (Ryu et al., 2015), and to that estimated from a bulk fluorescence dequenching assay (~1/20 s−1) (Cipriano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published rates from cited studies.

claim: The disassembly rate of L-SNARE-CC is comparable to that estimated from a bulk fluorescence dequenching assay (~1/20 s−1).
source: This disassembly rate is comparable to that previously observed by smFRET experiments using unlinked SNARE complexes reconstituted in liposomes (1/14 s−1) (Ryu et al., 2015), and to that estimated from a bulk fluorescence dequenching assay (~1/20 s−1) (Cipriano et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with previously published rates from cited studies.

claim: The activity of NSF/αSNAP is sensitive to the ionic strength of the solution.
source: As previously reported, the activity of NSF/αSNAP is sensitive to the ionic strength of the solution (Cipriano et al., 2013; Vivona et al., 2013; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Increasing the NaCl concentration led to a larger fraction of molecules that did not undergo transitions.
source: Indeed, in our smFRET assay, increasing the NaCl concentration led to a larger fraction of molecules that did not undergo transitions (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: The probability of low FRET efficiency decreased for molecules with transitions when NaCl concentration was increased.
source: Moreover, the probability of low FRET efficiency decreased for the remaining molecules with transitions (Figure 3B), and the long-lived dwell times for high FRET efficiency increased (note the shift of the right maximum in Figure 3D), consistent with expectation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The long-lived dwell times for high FRET efficiency increased when NaCl concentration was increased.
source: Moreover, the probability of low FRET efficiency decreased for the remaining molecules with transitions (Figure 3B), and the long-lived dwell times for high FRET efficiency increased (note the shift of the right maximum in Figure 3D), consistent with expectation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The populations of long-lived dwell times for low FRET decreased while the short-lived population increased when NaCl concentration was increased.
source: Finally, the populations of long-lived dwell times for low FRET decreased while the short-lived population increased (Figure 3E), (i.e., most occurrences of low FRET efficiency are single spikes in the time traces) (Figure 3A, right subpanel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: NSF activity is highly dependent upon αSNAP concentration.
source: NSF activity is highly dependent upon αSNAP concentration (Clary et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The disassembly rate in a bulk assay decreases as the αSNAP concentration is lowered.
source: For example, the disassembly rate in a bulk assay decreases as the αSNAP concentration is lowered (Vivona et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Decreasing the αSNAP concentration resulted in an increase in molecules without transitions.
source: In our smFRET assay, decreasing the αSNAP concentration had similar effects as increasing ionic strength (Figure 3F–J), as lowering the αSNAP concentration resulted in an increase in molecules without transitions (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The probability of low point-wise FRET efficiency decreased for molecules with transitions when αSNAP concentration was decreased.
source: Furthermore, the probability of low point-wise FRET efficiency decreased for the remaining molecules with transitions (Figure 3G), and the population of long-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency decreased (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The population of long-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency decreased when αSNAP concentration was decreased.
source: Furthermore, the probability of low point-wise FRET efficiency decreased for the remaining molecules with transitions (Figure 3G), and the population of long-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency decreased (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: At 0.5 µM αSNAP, only 25% of the SNARE complex is expected to be bound to αSNAP.
source: This decrease in NSF-mediated disassembly activity is expected considering the dissociation constant of 1.5 µM between αSNAP and the SNARE complex (Vivona et al., 2013); at 0.5 µM αSNAP, only 25% of the SNARE complex is expected to be bound to αSNAP, while at 20 µM, 93% is bound.
evidence: This is calculated based on the known dissociation constant from a cited study.

claim: At 20 µM αSNAP, 93% of the SNARE complex is expected to be bound to αSNAP.
source: This decrease in NSF-mediated disassembly activity is expected considering the dissociation constant of 1.5 µM between αSNAP and the SNARE complex (Vivona et al., 2013); at 0.5 µM αSNAP, only 25% of the SNARE complex is expected to be bound to αSNAP, while at 20 µM, 93% is bound.
evidence: This is calculated based on the known dissociation constant from a cited study.

claim: The KK mutant of αSNAP (K122E, K163E) abolished disassembly activity.
source: As expected, and consistent with previous results, the KK mutant of αSNAP abolished disassembly activity, while the EEED mutant had a milder effect (Figure 4B–D) (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D and is consistent with previous results from a cited study.

claim: The EEED mutant of αSNAP (E39A, E40A, E43A, D80A) had a milder effect on disassembly activity compared to the KK mutant.
source: As expected, and consistent with previous results, the KK mutant of αSNAP abolished disassembly activity, while the EEED mutant had a milder effect (Figure 4B–D) (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-D and is consistent with previous results from a cited study.

claim: No transitions were observed for the KK mutant of αSNAP.
source: Specifically, no transitions were observed for the KK mutant, while for the EEED mutant, the number molecules without transitions increased 2.5-fold compared to wildtype αSNAP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For the EEED mutant of αSNAP, the number of molecules without transitions increased 2.5-fold compared to wildtype αSNAP.
source: Specifically, no transitions were observed for the KK mutant, while for the EEED mutant, the number molecules without transitions increased 2.5-fold compared to wildtype αSNAP (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: For the EEED mutant of αSNAP, the distribution of the long-lived dwell times for the high FRET efficiency state shifted to longer times.
source: Moreover, for the EEED mutant, the distribution of the long-lived dwell times for the high FRET efficiency state shifted to longer times (Figure 4E) while the population of short-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency state increased and shifted towards shorter times (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For the EEED mutant of αSNAP, the population of short-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency state increased and shifted towards shorter times.
source: Moreover, for the EEED mutant, the distribution of the long-lived dwell times for the high FRET efficiency state shifted to longer times (Figure 4E) while the population of short-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency state increased and shifted towards shorter times (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The fraction of molecules without transitions and the point-wise FRET probability distributions are similar for L-SNAREfull-CC and L-SNARE-CC constructs.
source: The fraction of molecules without transitions and the point-wise FRET probability distributions are similar to those of the Habc-free L-SNARE-CC construct (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: The short- and long-lived dwell time populations are similar for L-SNAREfull-CC and L-SNARE-CC constructs.
source: Moreover, the short- and long-lived dwell time populations are similar (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The distributions of the long-lived dwell times for both high and low FRET efficiency shifted to longer times when the Habc domain was present.
source: Interestingly, however, the distributions of the long-lived dwell times for both high and low FRET efficiency shifted to longer times, indicating that the Habc domain reduces both disassembly and assembly rates of the SNARE complex (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The Habc domain reduces both disassembly and assembly rates of the SNARE complex.
source: Interestingly, however, the distributions of the long-lived dwell times for both high and low FRET efficiency shifted to longer times, indicating that the Habc domain reduces both disassembly and assembly rates of the SNARE complex (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed shift in dwell time distributions shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The effect of Cpx was similar to decreasing the αSNAP concentration or increasing the ionic strength of the disassembly buffer.
source: Overall, the effect of Cpx was similar to decreasing the αSNAP concentration or increasing the ionic strength of the disassembly buffer.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental results across different conditions.

claim: Increasing the Cpx concentration resulted in an increase in molecules without transitions.
source: Specifically, increasing the Cpx concentration resulted in an increase in molecules without transitions (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The probability of low point-wise FRET efficiency decreased for molecules with transitions when Cpx concentration was increased.
source: The probability of low point-wise FRET efficiency decreased for the remaining molecules with transitions (Figure 6C), and the population of long-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency decreased (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The population of long-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency decreased when Cpx concentration was increased.
source: The probability of low point-wise FRET efficiency decreased for the remaining molecules with transitions (Figure 6C), and the population of long-lived dwell times for low FRET efficiency decreased (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: At 10 μM concentration, the 4M mutant of Cpx has intermediate effects on the point-wise FRET distribution and the number of molecules without transitions.
source: At 10 μM concentration, this mutant has intermediate effects on the point-wise FRET distribution and the number of molecules without transitions, while the dwell time distributions are similar to those without Cpx (Figure 6B–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-F.

claim: The dwell time distributions for the 4M mutant of Cpx at 10 μM are similar to those without Cpx.
source: At 10 μM concentration, this mutant has intermediate effects on the point-wise FRET distribution and the number of molecules without transitions, while the dwell time distributions are similar to those without Cpx (Figure 6B–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-F.

claim: Cpx competes with αSNAP binding to the SNARE complex, with the most significant effect observed at Cpx:αSNAP molar ratios ≥ 1.
source: Cpx competes with αSNAP binding to the SNARE complex, with the most significant effect observed at Cpx:αSNAP molar ratios ≥ 1.
evidence: This is supported by competition binding experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The 4M mutant of Cpx has only a mild effect on αSNAP binding, comparable to the effect of wild type Cpx at a hundred-fold lower concentration (0.1 μM).
source: In contrast, the 4M mutant of Cpx has only a mild effect on αSNAP binding, comparable to the effect of wild type Cpx at a hundred-fold lower concentration (0.1 μM).
evidence: This is supported by competition binding experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: NSF disassembles the binary t-SNARE complex composed of syntaxin-1A and SNAP-25A.
source: In addition to the ternary SNARE complex, NSF also disassembles the binary t-SNARE complex composed of syntaxin-1A and SNAP-25A (Lai et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Intermediate FRET efficiency was observed in the point-wise probability distributions for both L-SNAREbinary-CC1 and L-SNAREbinary-CC2.
source: In contrast to the linked ternary SNARE complex L-SNARE-CC, we observed intermediate FRET efficiency in the point-wise probability distributions for both L-SNAREbinary-CC1 and L-SNAREbinary-CC2 (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: A sum of three Gaussian distributions provides a reasonable fit to the point-wise FRET efficiency distributions for binary SNARE complexes, supporting the notion of three distinct states.
source: We therefore fit a sum of three Gaussian distributions to the point-wise FRET efficiency distributions (Figure 7C–D), resulting in a reasonable fit supporting the notion of three distinct states (with low, mid, and high FRET efficiency) for the binary SNARE complex.
evidence: This is supported by fitting analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: The fraction of molecules without transitions for both L-SNAREbinary-CC1 and L-SNAREbinary-CC2 was similar.
source: The fraction of molecules without transitions for both L-SNAREbinary-CC1 and L-SNAREbinary-CC2 was similar (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Compared to ternary L-SNARE-CC, the occurrence of long-lived dwell times decreased for binary SNARE complexes.
source: Compared to ternary L-SNARE-CC, the occurrence of long-lived dwell times decreased (red dots in Figures 2F and 7F–G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figures 2F and 7F-G.

claim: The populations of the long-lived dwell times for both mid and low FRET efficiency decreased slightly for binary SNARE complexes.
source: The populations of the long-lived dwell times for both mid and low FRET efficiency decreased slightly (Figure 7H–I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H-I.

claim: The FRET efficiency time traces for both L-SNAREbinary-CC1 and L-SNAREbinary-CC2 did not show any conformational transitions (except for photobleaching events) in the absence of the disassembly factors.
source: As a control, the FRET efficiency time traces for both L-SNAREbinary-CC1 and L-SNAREbinary-CC2 did not show any conformational transitions (except for photobleaching events) in the absence of the disassembly factors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) in agreement with previous observations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The distribution of point-wise FRET efficiencies is indicative of at least three conformations of the binary t-SNARE complex (fully assembled, or with either of the two SNAP-25A domains dislodged).
source: Furthermore, the distribution of point-wise FRET efficiencies is indicative of at least three conformations of the binary t-SNARE complex (fully assembled, or with either of the two SNAP-25A domains dislodged) (Weninger et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRET data supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The kinetics of NSF-mediated SNARE complex disassembly are largely independent of the choice of FRET labeling pairs.
source: Thus, the kinetics of NSF-mediated SNARE complex disassembly are largely independent of the choice of FRET labeling pairs, enabling comparison of the dissembly of SNARE complexes labeled at different positions.
evidence: This is based on comparison of experimental data from different labeling constructs shown in Figure 8.

claim: Differences in the point-wise FRET distributions for different labeling pairs can be explained by variations in distances for these labeling pairs in both the assembled and disassembled SNARE complexes.
source: Differences in the point-wise FRET distributions can be explained by variations in distances for these labeling pairs in both the assembled and disassembled SNARE complexes (Figure 8B–C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known relationship between FRET efficiency and distance.

claim: Differences in the percentage of molecules without transitions for different labeling pairs are likely due to variation in the efficiency with which 20S complex forms.
source: There are also differences in the percentage of molecules without transitions (Figure 8D); these are likely due to variation in the efficiency with which 20S complex forms (i.e., some of the dye combinations may differentially affect the assembly of the 20S complex).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for observed differences in the data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The dwell time distributions and the short- and long-lived populations are similar for different FRET labeling pairs.
source: Nevertheless, the dwell time distributions and the short- and long-lived populations are similar (Figure 8E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8E-F.

claim: When SNARE proteins are simply mixed in the absence of Munc18 and Munc13, they are sometimes kinetically trapped in nonproductive (e.g., anti-parallel) configurations.
source: When the SNARE proteins are simply mixed in the absence of Munc18 and Munc13, they are sometimes kinetically trapped in nonproductive (e.g., anti-parallel) configurations (Choi et al., 2016; Lai et al., 2017; Sakon and Weninger, 2010; Weninger et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Molecules purified without a urea wash were observed in both stable parallel and anti-parallel configurations.
source: Consistent with previous observations (Choi et al., 2016; Weninger et al., 2003), molecules purifed without a urea wash were observed in both stable parallel and anti-parallel configurations (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B) in the absence of the urea wash.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A,B and citations to previous work.

claim: When the purification protocol included a urea wash step prior to surface tethering, L-SNARE-CN molecules were mostly found in the proper parallel configuration.
source: When the purification protocol included a urea wash step prior to surface tethering, L-SNARE-CN molecules were mostly found in the proper parallel configuration (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the presence of disassembly factors, the smFRET efficiency time traces of the anti-parallel-reporting L-SNARE-CN molecules showed brief transitions to high FRET efficiency corresponding to improperly assembled anti-parallel configurations.
source: In the presence of disassembly factors, the smFRET efficiency time traces of the anti-parallel-reporting L-SNARE-CN molecules showed brief transitions to high FRET efficiency corresponding to improperly assembled anti-parallel configurations (Figure 9B–C, Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B-C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Improperly assembled SNARE-CN molecules were rapidly disassembled by NSF.
source: These improperly assembled SNARE-CN molecules were then rapidly disassembled by NSF as indicated by the subsequent disappearance of high FRET efficiency (Figure 9B), while they remained in the high-FRET efficiency configuration in the absence of disassembly factors (Figure 9—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9B and Figure 9—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Nearly 50% of the dwell times for high FRET efficiency states of anti-parallel configurations were short-lived (< 0.56 s).
source: Nearly 50% of the dwell times for high FRET efficiency states were short-lived (< 0.56 s, Figure 9F), indicating a rapid NSF-mediated disassembly of anti-parallel configurations.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: NSF is capable of disassembling improperly assembled anti-parallel SNARE complexes on a timescale faster than that of properly assembled ternary SNARE complexes.
source: Taken together, our data show that NSF is capable of disassembling improperly assembled anti-parallel SNARE complexes on a timescale faster than that of properly assembled ternary SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of experimental data for anti-parallel and parallel SNARE complexes.

claim: The linked form of the SNARE complex allows observation of multiple rounds of NSF-mediated disassembly and reassembly of the same molecule.
source: Additionally, we studied a linked form of the SNARE complex, allowing us to observe multiple rounds of NSF-mediated disassembly and reassembly of the same molecule.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing multiple transitions in smFRET traces.

claim: The linked SNARE complex approach distinguishes between true molecular events and events that are due to photophysics, such as photobleaching.
source: This approach also distinguishes between true molecular events and events that are due to photophysics, such as photobleaching.
evidence: This is a methodological advantage of the linked SNARE approach described in the manuscript.

claim: The disassembly rates of the tethered and linked SNARE complexes (L-SNARE-CC molecules) obtained from the smFRET assay are similar to those measured in solution by other assays.
source: As expected, the disassembly rates of the tethered and linked SNARE complexes (L-SNARE-CC molecules) obtained from our smFRET assay are similar to those measured in solution by other assays.
evidence: This is based on comparison with previously published rates from other assays.

claim: The smFRET assay reveals two temporal states for both SNARE complex disassembly and reassembly for the first time.
source: For the first time, our smFRET assay reveals two temporal states for both SNARE complex disassembly and reassembly (Figure 2G–H), with the large majority of the SNARE complexes found in the long-lived states.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: The large majority of the SNARE complexes are found in the long-lived states.
source: For the first time, our smFRET assay reveals two temporal states for both SNARE complex disassembly and reassembly (Figure 2G–H), with the large majority of the SNARE complexes found in the long-lived states.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-H.

claim: With respect to disassembly, the long-lived states represent complete NSF-mediated disassembly.
source: With respect to disassembly, these long-lived states represent complete NSF-mediated disassembly, while the short-lived states are failed disassembly or disassembly followed by immediate reassembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data based on the dwell time distributions.

claim: With respect to disassembly, the short-lived states are failed disassembly or disassembly followed by immediate reassembly.
source: With respect to disassembly, these long-lived states represent complete NSF-mediated disassembly, while the short-lived states are failed disassembly or disassembly followed by immediate reassembly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data based on the dwell time distributions.

claim: With respect to assembly, the short-lived state may correspond to a partially assembled SNARE complex that reverts to the disassembled state.
source: As for assembly, the short-lived state may correspond to a partially assembled SNARE complex (e.g., with one or more of the SNARE motifs not being fully incorporated) that reverts to the disassembled state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: High ionic strength, low αSNAP concentration, mutation of charged residues of αSNAP involved in SNARE complex binding, or addition of Cpx all have similar effects on SNARE complex disassembly.
source: High ionic strength, low αSNAP concentration, mutation of charged residues of αSNAP involved in SNARE complex binding, or addition of Cpx all have similar effects.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings from multiple conditions tested.

claim: In each case (high ionic strength, low αSNAP concentration, αSNAP mutations, or Cpx addition), fewer SNARE complexes are disassembled, and the disassembly dwell times for SNARE complexes are shorter.
source: In each case, fewer SNARE complexes are disassembled, and the disassembly dwell times for SNARE complexes are shorter (Figures 3–4 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3-4 and 6.

claim: The presence of the syntaxin-1A N-terminal Habc domain slowed both the disassembly and reassembly processes slightly.
source: We also found that the presence of the syntaxin-1A N-terminal Habc domain slowed both the disassembly and reassembly processes slightly (Figure 5), which may be explained by hindrance effects of the Habc domain on both formation of the 20S complex and on spontaneous reassembly of the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The slowing effect of the Habc domain may be explained by hindrance effects on both formation of the 20S complex and on spontaneous reassembly of the SNARE complex.
source: We also found that the presence of the syntaxin-1A N-terminal Habc domain slowed both the disassembly and reassembly processes slightly (Figure 5), which may be explained by hindrance effects of the Habc domain on both formation of the 20S complex and on spontaneous reassembly of the SNARE complex.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed effects of the Habc domain.

claim: Previous reports differed on the effect of Cpx on SNARE complex disassembly in bulk.
source: Previous reports differed on the effect of Cpx on SNARE complex disassembly in bulk (Pabst et al., 2000; Winter et al., 2009); in retrospect, these differing results can be explained by different αSNAP:Cpx molar ratios.
evidence: This is a statement about the literature supported by citations.

claim: At an αSNAP:Cpx ratio of ~18:1, Cpx had no effect on SNARE complex disassembly.
source: At a ratio of ~18:1, Cpx had no effect (Pabst et al., 2000), whereas at a ratio of ~3:1, Cpx had a substantial effect on NSF-mediated disassembly of the soluble SNARE complex (Winter et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: At an αSNAP:Cpx ratio of ~3:1, Cpx had a substantial effect on NSF-mediated disassembly of the soluble SNARE complex.
source: At a ratio of ~18:1, Cpx had no effect (Pabst et al., 2000), whereas at a ratio of ~3:1, Cpx had a substantial effect on NSF-mediated disassembly of the soluble SNARE complex (Winter et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The presence of a membrane reduced the inhibitory effect of Cpx on NSF-mediated disassembly, presumably due to an effective local concentration increase of αSNAP as a result of its interaction with the membrane.
source: The presence of a membrane reduced the inhibitory effect by Cpx, presumably due to an effective local concentration increase of αSNAP as a result of its interaction with the membrane (Winter et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and includes a speculative explanation.

claim: All these results point to a critical role of αSNAP and its precise stoichiometry in the NSF-mediated disassembly activity.
source: All these results point to a critical role of αSNAP and its precise stoichiometry in the NSF-mediated disassembly activity, as discussed below.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: A recent EM structure of the 20S complex allowed unique assignment of the positions of the individual SNARE components and their interactions with αSNAP molecules.
source: A recent EM structure of the 20S complex allowed unique assignment of the positions of the individual SNARE components and their interactions with αSNAP molecules (White et al., 2018) revealing that two αSNAP molecules bind primarily to a portion of the surface formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 in the ternary SNARE complex (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study.

claim: Two αSNAP molecules bind primarily to a portion of the surface formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 in the ternary SNARE complex.
source: A recent EM structure of the 20S complex allowed unique assignment of the positions of the individual SNARE components and their interactions with αSNAP molecules (White et al., 2018) revealing that two αSNAP molecules bind primarily to a portion of the surface formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 in the ternary SNARE complex (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study and the structure shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The EM structure of the L-20S complex reported here is similar to that of the recent EM structure of the neuronal 20S complex and the V7-20S complex.
source: The EM structure of the L-20S complex reported here is similar to that of the recent EM structure of both the neuronal 20S complex (White et al., 2018) and the V7-20S complex (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison of the structure determined in this study with previously published structures.

claim: This intermolecular interaction (between αSNAP and syntaxin-1A/synaptobrevin-2) has also been observed in another structure of the 20S complex that contained four αSNAP molecules.
source: Moreover, this intermolecular interaction has also been observed in another structure of the 20S complex that contained four αSNAP molecules (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study.

claim: All structures of 20S complex determined thus far contain a conserved structural motif consisting of two αSNAP molecules that interact with a portion of the surface formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptovrevin-2 in the ternary SNARE complex.
source: While there is at present no evidence that a 20S complex cannot form with only one αSNAP molecule, all structures of 20S complex determined thus far contain a conserved structural motif consisting of two αSNAP molecules that interact with a portion of the surface formed by syntaxin-1A and synaptovrevin-2 in the ternary SNARE complex.
evidence: This is a summary statement about all available structural data on the 20S complex.

claim: Complexin binds to the groove between syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 helices in the SNARE complex.
source: Structurally, Cpx binds to the groove between syntaxin-1A and synaptobrevin-2 helices in the SNARE complex (Chen et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous structural study.

claim: Superposition of the structure of the αSNAP/L-SNARE subcomplex of the L-20S complex with that of the SNARE/Cpx complex suggests that Cpx competes with one of the two αSNAP molecules.
source: Superposition of the structure of the αSNAP/L-SNARE subcomplex of the L-20S complex with that of the SNARE/Cpx complex suggests that Cpx competes with one of the two αSNAP molecules (Figure 6G), as corroborated by a competition assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 6G and supported by competition assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At least two αSNAPs are required for a key step of productive disassembly.
source: Because Cpx interferes with binding of only one of the two αSNAPs to the SNARE complex, this suggests that at least two αSNAPs are required for a key step of productive disassembly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that Cpx competes with one αSNAP and inhibits disassembly.

claim: If only one αSNAP is present, disassembly might not proceed to completion, as suggested by the presence of the low FRET efficiency spikes in smFRET experiments.
source: If only one αSNAP is present, disassembly might not proceed to completion, as suggested by the presence of the low FRET efficiency spikes in our smFRET experiments (Figures 2J and 6F).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on experimental data shown in Figures 2J and 6F.

claim: A third αSNAP molecule may be engaged during the hydrolysis cycle.
source: Moreover, a third αSNAP molecule may be engaged during the hydrolysis cycle (Shah et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: In the neuron, there are approximately similar expression levels of Cpx, αSNAP, γSNAP, and to a lesser degree, βSNAP.
source: In the neuron, there are approximately similar expression levels of Cpx, αSNAP, γSNAP, and to a lesser degree, βSNAP (Clary et al., 1990; Nishiki et al., 2001; Söllner et al., 1993a; Whiteheart et al., 1992; Wilhelm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on protein expression levels.

claim: At a 1:1 molar ratio of Cpx to αSNAP, there is little NSF-mediated disassembly of the SNARE complex in smFRET experiments.
source: At a 1:1 molar ratio of Cpx to αSNAP, there is little NSF-mediated disassembly of the SNARE complex in our smFRET experiments (see 10 μM Cpx, Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Because the concentration of SNAPs in the neuron is roughly three times higher than that of Cpx, some disassembly would take place assuming similar affinities and activities of all SNAP isoforms.
source: However, because the concentration of SNAPs in the neuron is roughly three times higher than that of Cpx, some disassembly would take place assuming similar affinities and activities of all SNAP isoforms.
evidence: This is an inference based on known protein concentrations in neurons.

claim: Membrane binding of αSNAP might further increase the local SNAP concentration at the plasma membrane where cis SNARE complexes are present, thus mitigating a possible inhibitory effect of Cpx on NSF-mediated cis SNARE complex disassembly.
source: Moreover, membrane binding of αSNAP (Winter et al., 2009) might further increase the local SNAP concentration at the plasma membrane where cis SNARE complexes are present, thus mitigating a possible inhibitory effect of Cpx on NSF-mediated cis SNARE complex disassembly.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to previous research on αSNAP membrane binding.

claim: Sequestration of Cpx to the synaptic vesicle via its curvature sensing C-terminal domain may increase the local Cpx concentration, effectively decreasing the local SNAP:Cpx molar ratio and leading to inhibition of unwanted NSF-mediated disassembly of trans SNARE complexes.
source: On the other hand, sequestration of Cpx to the synaptic vesicle via its curvature sensing C-terminal domain (Gong et al., 2016) may increase the local Cpx concentration, effectively decreasing the local SNAP:Cpx molar ratio and leading to inhibition of unwanted NSF-mediated disassembly of trans SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to previous research on Cpx localization.

claim: An atomic force microscopy study reported that the stability of an anti-parallel ternary SNARE complex is three-fold lower than the properly assembled parallel complex.
source: Interestingly, an atomic force microscopy study reported that the stability of an anti-parallel ternary SNARE complex is three-fold lower than the properly assembled parallel complex (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The fast disassembly rate observed for anti-parallel configurations is speculated to be related to their lower stability.
source: We speculate that the fast disassembly rate observed for anti-parallel configurations is related to their lower stability.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed fast disassembly of anti-parallel SNARE complexes.

claim: Relatively long-lived intermediate states were revealed during NSF-mediated disassembly of the binary t-SNARE complex.
source: Using the binary t-SNARE (syntaxin-1A/SNAP-25A) complex as an example, we also studied the disassembly of incomplete SNARE complexes. Our experiments revealed the presence of relatively long-lived intermediate states during NSF-mediated disassembly of the binary t-SNARE complex (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Occasionally, the system reverted to the previous state instead of proceeding to full disassembly during binary t-SNARE disassembly.
source: Occasionally, the system reverted to the previous state instead of proceeding to full disassembly (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Intermediate states were observed during spontaneous reassembly of binary t-SNARE complexes.
source: Similarly, we observed such intermediates during spontaneous reassembly.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations of the binary t-SNARE complex.

claim: Intermediate states during NSF-mediated disassembly of the ternary SNARE complex were not observed, but they may occur on a faster timescale (faster than 100 msec) than is currently observable.
source: Although we did not observe intermediate states during NSF-mediated disassembly of the ternary SNARE complex (Figure 2), they may occur on a faster timescale (i.e., faster than 100 msec) than is currently observable with our apparatus.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of observed intermediates in ternary SNARE complex disassembly.

claim: Single-molecule experiments revealed two temporal states (short- and long-lived) of SNARE complexes for both NSF-mediated disassembly and spontaneous reassembly that are influenced by various conditions.
source: Our single-molecule experiments revealed two temporal states (short- and long-lived) of SNARE complexes for both NSF-mediated disassembly and spontaneous reassembly that are influenced by various conditions, such as αSNAP and Cpx concentration.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the single-molecule experiments.

claim: The long-lived states represent stable assembled and disassembled states of the SNARE complex.
source: The long-lived states represent stable assembled and disassembled states of the SNARE complex, while the short-lived states represent incomplete or improper states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The short-lived states represent incomplete or improper states of the SNARE complex.
source: The long-lived states represent stable assembled and disassembled states of the SNARE complex, while the short-lived states represent incomplete or improper states.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Future technical improvements may expand the accessible timescales of the assay, enabling further dissection of the short-lived transitions.
source: Future technical improvements may expand the accessible timescales of the assay, enabling further dissection of the short-lived transitions.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future work.

claim: The approach could be useful in the study of the effect of other accessory proteins in the disassembly process.
source: Furthermore, our approach could be useful not only in the study of the effect of other accessory proteins in the disassembly process, but also in the study of the motions of NSF correlated with disassembly through analysis of intermolecular FRET between labeled SNARE complex and NSF.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the method.

claim: The approach could be useful in the study of the motions of NSF correlated with disassembly through analysis of intermolecular FRET between labeled SNARE complex and NSF.
source: Furthermore, our approach could be useful not only in the study of the effect of other accessory proteins in the disassembly process, but also in the study of the motions of NSF correlated with disassembly through analysis of intermolecular FRET between labeled SNARE complex and NSF.
evidence: This is a statement about potential future applications of the method.

claim: Together with the static structures from X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, the dynamics extracted from smFRET studies will ultimately provide a more complete understanding of the molecular mechanism of NSF-mediated disassembly of the SNARE complex.
source: Together with the static structures from X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, the dynamics extracted from these smFRET studies will ultimately provide a more complete understanding of the molecular mechanism of NSF-mediated disassembly of the SNARE complex, an essential process in the membrane fusion cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about the broader significance of combining structural and dynamic studies.

claim: NSF-mediated disassembly of the SNARE complex is an essential process in the membrane fusion cycle.
source: Together with the static structures from X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, the dynamics extracted from these smFRET studies will ultimately provide a more complete understanding of the molecular mechanism of NSF-mediated disassembly of the SNARE complex, an essential process in the membrane fusion cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological importance of the process being studied.

claim: The reconstructed density map of the L-20S complex has an estimated resolution of 7.0 Å without imposing any symmetry after refinement with RELION.
source: The reconstructed density map of the L-20S complex has an estimated resolution of 7.0 Å without imposing any symmetry after refinement with RELION (Scheres, 2012) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a technical detail about the cryo-EM structure determination shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Anti-parallel SNARE complexes are disassembled at a faster rate than properly assembled ternary SNARE complexes.
source: Critically, we find that off-target, anti-parallel SNARE complexes and binary (t-SNARE) complexes are disassembled at a faster rate than properly assembled ternary SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing disassembly rates of different SNARE complex configurations.

claim: Binary (t-SNARE) complexes are disassembled at a faster rate than properly assembled ternary SNARE complexes.
source: Critically, we find that off-target, anti-parallel SNARE complexes and binary (t-SNARE) complexes are disassembled at a faster rate than properly assembled ternary SNARE complexes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing disassembly rates of different SNARE complex configurations.

claim: The addition of the high-affinity binding factor Cpx partially interferes with NSF-mediated disassembly.
source: Finally, the addition of the high-affinity binding factor Cpx partially interferes with NSF-mediated disassembly.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the effect of Cpx on disassembly kinetics.
